outcome: The general conjecture (infinitely many real quadratic fields with class number one) remains open; all work found since 26 January 2024 either studies specific parametric families, proves bounds/indivisibility results for class numbers of real quadratic fields, or is a single uncorroborated preprint claiming a full solution that shows no sign of expert acceptance.

disputes.summary: Igor V. Nikolaev posted arXiv:2512.02232 ('Lambert W-function and Gauss class number one conjecture', 1 December 2025) claiming to derive a solution to the Gauss conjecture for real quadratic fields of class number one, via fixed points of a function built from Drinfeld-module representations as bounded operators on a Hilbert space. No journal acceptance, expert digestion, citation, or community endorsement of this claim was found. Nikolaev has a long arXiv history of similar unconventional operator-algebra/noncommutative-geometry claims about famous open conjectures that have not been accepted by the number theory community. A May 2026 AIM/Harmonic/AWS/NSF workshop on 'AI and Number Theory' (5 months after the preprint) still listed the Gauss real-quadratic class-number conjecture as an open target problem for AI attack, which is inconsistent with the community having accepted Nikolaev's claim as a resolution.

summary: The Gauss conjecture that infinitely many real quadratic fields have class number one is still listed as open by Wikipedia's own Class number problem article as of this research, and is treated as open in the number-theory literature searched. Work published in the window addresses adjacent but distinct questions under the §3.1 scope rule: Bernardini (arXiv:2412.06351, Dec 2024) proves h(D)>1 for a specific family of real quadratic fields with known continued-fraction expansions (all but finitely many exceptions) — this is evidence about a family, not a case of the infinitude conjecture, and if anything narrows where class-number-one fields in that family could occur, rather than settling the existence question (per §3.1's rule that infinitude questions move only when answered). A 2025 paper (arXiv:2506.21301) improves an upper bound (Yamamoto 1971) on how many real quadratic fields below a given discriminant have small class number, again a bound on a distribution, not the infinitude conjecture itself. A 2025 machine-learning paper (arXiv:2209.09283, actually from 2022, predating the window and thus irrelevant here) used supervised learning to rediscover Cohen–Lenstra-type patterns in class-number data, but is neither in-window nor does it touch the infinitude question; it was surfaced by triage but is out of scope both by date and by topic. The one item that looked like it could change the status is Igor Nikolaev's December 2025 preprint (arXiv:2512.02232) explicitly claiming 'a solution to the Gauss conjecture for the real quadratic fields of class number one' via noncommutative-geometry/Drinfeld-module methods. I read the abstract and available content; there is no digestion by experts, no citations, no journal acceptance, and Nikolaev has a documented pattern of posting similar claims about other famous conjectures using the same toolkit without community acceptance. Most tellingly, an AIM-sponsored 'AI and Number Theory' workshop convened in May 2026 — five months after this preprint — explicitly lists the Gauss real-quadratic class-number conjecture as an open problem suitable for AI attack, which would be a strange thing to do if the community had accepted a solution five months earlier. I therefore classify this preprint as an uncorroborated, likely-erroneous claim that does not meet even the `claimed` bar (which requires the claim to be a live candidate under some scrutiny) and does not change the `open` status; I note it fully in `disputes` rather than silently dropping it, per §7's instruction that priority/attribution and credibility disputes belong there. No AI system was found to be involved in any of the results located — the Bernardini and bound-improvement papers are conventional analytic/algebraic number theory, and no source claims AI assistance in producing the Nikolaev preprint's argument either. Overall: nothing has happened to the conjecture itself in the window, and there is no genuine AI involvement to report.
competing_reading: If a downstream reader wanted to be more generous to the Nikolaev preprint, one could argue for `status: claimed` with `resolution_direction: confirmed` (since the claim is that infinitely many such fields exist, matching Gauss's conjectured direction) and `ai_role: none`. I did not take this reading because `claimed` implies a live, still-being-evaluated claim, and I found zero evidence of the mathematical community treating it as such — no discussion, no citations, no follow-up, and a subsequent major workshop treating the problem as still open. Given Nikolaev's track record of similar claims on other famous problems (e.g., other operator-algebra 'proofs' of open conjectures) that were never accepted, I judged the more defensible reading to be that this is noise rather than a genuine claim in play, but a reader who weighs the mere existence of an unretracted, unwithdrawn preprint more heavily could reasonably classify it as `claimed`.
what_would_settle_it: Any expert commentary (blog post, MathOverflow thread, journal referee report, or citation) engaging substantively with arXiv:2512.02232 — either endorsing it, refuting it, or noting a withdrawal — would resolve whether it belongs in the record as `claimed` or should be dismissed entirely. Absent that, the paper's silence in the literature five-plus months after posting, and its omission from the AIM workshop's framing of the problem as open, is the best available evidence that it has not been accepted.
